title: Five remembrances
hookLine: I will age, sicken, die, be parted from what I love, and I am heir to my deeds

cards: A list short enough to fit on a card, and meant for everyone: man or woman, householder or monk. The Buddha says these five things should be reflected on often.
They're the medicine for something met four days ago, the three intoxications: the pride of being young, of being well, of being alive, which makes people careless.

teach.b: Here are the five, in plain words. One: I am of the nature to age; I haven't gone beyond aging. Two: I am of the nature to get sick; I haven't gone beyond sickness.
Three: I am of the nature to die; I haven't gone beyond death.

Four: everything and everyone dear to me will change, and I will be parted from them. Five: I am the owner of my deeds, heir to my deeds, born of my deeds, bound to my deeds; whatever I do, good or bad, I will inherit it.
It sounds grim. But the sutta explains why each line helps.

teach.h: EACH ONE WEARS DOWN A PRIDE.
teach.b: Thinking on aging wears down the pride of youth. On sickness, the pride of health. On death, the pride of being alive.

On parting, the clinging to what's dear. And thinking on deeds wears down misconduct in body, speech and mind. The first four are about what you can't control; the fifth is about the one thing you can.
That's the turn. You can't stop the clock or keep everyone forever, but what you do today becomes what you inherit.
Heir is the key word: like an estate, your deeds are passed down to you, the good with the bad. In some monasteries and homes, these five are chanted as a daily reflection.

how: Some Buddhist monasteries and lay groups recite the five remembrances as part of morning or evening chanting, and teachers offer them as a reflection for anyone, ordained or not.

o: five memories of the Buddha's past lives
five vows a lay follower takes for life
five daily reflections on age, loss and deeds

p: wears down the pride of youth
wears down the pride of health
wears down the pride of life

s: the five remembrances are only for monks and nuns
the sutta says they're for everyone: women and men, householders and monastics.
the fifth remembrance is about deeds, not death
I am the owner and heir of my deeds.
the sutta says thinking on death makes people more careless
it says the opposite: it wears down the pride of being alive.

games.q: four of the five remembrances name things you can't change. what does the fifth name?
o: your deeds, which you will inherit.
games.why: the fifth turns the list around: you can't stop aging or loss, but your deeds are yours, and you're their heir.

practice: Let the breath settle, then say the lines inwardly, slowly, one every few breaths: I will grow old; I may grow ill; I will die; what I love will change, and I will part from it; I am heir to my deeds.
If a line feels heavy, stay with the breath until it softens, and let the last line point somewhere: what you do is yours to shape.

wordCard.voice: Five remembrances. Aging, sickness, death, parting, and deeds: the five things the Buddha asked everyone to reflect on often, to wear down pride and steady the hand. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali kammadayada: 'heir of kamma,' from kamma, deed, and dayada, heir.

carryVoice: Your line: heir to my deeds. Four lines name what passes, and one names what stays yours. A week of the Numbered Sayings, done.
